title: Few Words Before God, and the Emptiness of Wealth
summary: The Teacher turns from what he has seen to how a person should come before God: listen more than you speak, keep your vows, and fear God. He then observes layers of officials who exploit the poor, and he shows how the love of money never satisfies, how riches can be hoarded or lost, and how everyone leaves the world as naked as they came. He ends by commending the simple enjoyment of food, drink, and work as God's gift.
story: Chapter 4 ended with a king who rises from poverty and is soon forgotten, another picture of the futility the Teacher keeps finding under the sun. Here he steps back from observation to give direct counsel about worship, and the change of tone is striking: for the first time in the book he speaks in commands. Then he returns to his investigation, this time of money. The chapter holds the book's two great notes side by side. Wealth cannot fill the heart and cannot be carried past death, yet the same God who sets these limits also gives food, work, and the power to enjoy them. The next chapter will take up the darker case, a man who has everything and is not allowed to enjoy it.
historical: The chapter assumes a temple where people come to offer sacrifices and make vows, and a government in which officials watch over other officials all the way up to the king. The word translated province in verse 8 (medinah) was a common term for administrative districts in the Persian period, used often in Esther, Ezra, and Nehemiah, though it also appears in the account of Ahab's reign (1 Kings 20:14-19). Scholars who date the book to the Persian or early Greek period read the verse as a picture of an imperial bureaucracy in which each layer took its share of the harvest. Those who hold to Solomon's authorship point out that Solomon also divided Israel into districts under officials who supplied the royal household (1 Kings 4:7-19). On either reading the world is the same: taxes flow upward, and the farmer at the bottom has little recourse.
cultural:
A vow in ancient Israel was a voluntary promise to God, often made in a time of need, to give an offering or do some act if God answered. Nobody was required to make one, but once spoken it was binding. The Teacher's warning in verses 4 and 5 closely follows the law of Deuteronomy 23:21-23, which says that a vow to the LORD must be paid without delay and that it is no sin to refrain from vowing. The messenger of verse 6, before whom a person might claim the vow was a mistake, is probably a temple official or priest who came to collect what had been promised; Malachi 2:7 calls the priest the messenger of the LORD of Hosts. Some take the messenger to be an angel.

The sacrifice of fools in verse 1 reflects a concern that runs through the prophets: ritual offered without a listening heart. The Teacher prefers drawing near to listen, which in Hebrew also means to obey. Verse 15 echoes Job 1:21, where Job says he came naked from his mother's womb and will return naked, and Paul makes the same point in 1 Timothy 6:7. The worker's sweet sleep in verse 12 would have been familiar to a society in which most people did hard physical labor, and the rich man's sleeplessness reflects the worry that comes with goods that must be guarded.
literary: In the Hebrew Bible the first verse of this chapter is numbered 4:17, so Hebrew 5:1-19 matches English 5:2-20. The chapter falls into two parts. Verses 1 to 7 are instruction in the style of Proverbs, a series of commands with reasons attached, framed by the idea of drawing near to God and ending in the command “Therefore, fear God.” Dreams and words are paired twice (verses 3 and 7): as busy days produce restless dreams, so fools produce many words, and both are hevel, breath. Verses 8 to 20 return to the Teacher's first-person reflection, moving from the injustice of the system to the love of money, then to a case study (a man who loses his wealth in a failed venture and has nothing to leave his son), and finally to a counterweight: “Here is what I have seen to be good and fitting.” The chapter's last verse is ambiguous in Hebrew. It may mean that God keeps a person so occupied with joy that the brevity of life does not weigh on him, or that God answers a person through the joy of his heart.

outline.t: Draw near to listen; let your words be few
Keep your vows, and fear God
Officials over officials, and the oppression of the poor
The love of money never satisfies
Wealth hoarded, wealth lost, and the naked departure
Enjoyment of food and work as God's gift

doctrines.note: “God is in heaven and you are on earth” (5:2). The distance between Creator and creature calls for reverence, few words, and kept promises. Worship is first a matter of listening, not of impressing God with offerings or speeches.

The one who loves money is never satisfied by it (5:10). The Teacher describes the restlessness of a heart that asks wealth to be what only God can be, and he shows that such wealth cannot even be taken past the grave.

Riches, the ability to enjoy them, and the joy of the heart are all called God's gift (5:19-20). The same God who makes wealth unable to satisfy also gives the ordinary goods of life as a portion to be received with thanks.

words.note: Nadar, to vow. The verb and its noun appear together in verse 4. A vow was a freely chosen promise to God, and the whole weight of the passage falls on the gap between speaking and doing. The Teacher does not discourage vows; he discourages careless ones, since God takes a spoken promise seriously even when the person who made it does not.

Hevel, breath or vapor, translated futility here. It appears twice in this chapter: many dreams and many words are hevel (verse 7), and so is loving money that never satisfies (verse 10). Readers differ on whether the word stresses emptiness, brevity, or what cannot be grasped. In this chapter all three fit: words vanish, money slips away, and neither delivers what it promises.

Cheleq, portion or lot. The word was used for a share of land or plunder, something allotted. In verses 18 and 19 the Teacher calls eating, drinking, and satisfaction in work a person's lot. It is not everything a person might want, but it is a real share, given by God, and wisdom lies in receiving it rather than grasping for more.

Yare, to fear or revere. “Therefore, fear God” (5:7) is the practical conclusion of the section on worship and one of the book's key threads, which the epilogue will make its final word (12:13). The fear of God here is not terror but a sober awareness of who God is, which makes a person quiet, honest, and careful with promises.

christ: Jesus gave the same warnings in his own teaching. He told his disciples not to heap up empty phrases in prayer as though they would be heard for their many words (Matthew 6:7), and he taught that a plain yes or no is better than a flourish of oaths (Matthew 5:33-37), which James repeats (James 5:12). His parable of the rich fool, who built bigger barns and died that night, is a story version of verses 13 to 17 (Luke 12:13-21), and he warned that where your treasure is, there your heart will be also (Matthew 6:19-21). The link is thematic: the Teacher sees that wealth cannot be carried past death, and Jesus directs his hearers to treasure that can. He also fulfills what the Teacher says about true worship, for in him God, who is in heaven, has come to earth, and the listening the Teacher commends becomes listening to the Son (Mark 9:7).

hard.q: Does the Teacher tell us not to be surprised by injustice, as if to accept it?
hard.a: Verse 8 says that when you see the poor oppressed and justice denied in the province, you should not be astonished, because every official has a superior over him. Some read this as weary realism: corruption runs all the way up the chain, and each layer protects the one below. Others read it as a partial reassurance, that officials are watched and accountable, and they read verse 9 as saying that even the king depends on the land and so has an interest in its care. The Hebrew of verse 9 is difficult, and both readings have defenders. Either way, the Teacher is not approving oppression. He has already wept over the tears of the oppressed (4:1), and the book's conclusion that God will judge every deed (12:14) means the injustice he describes is not the last word. His point is that no one should be naive about power.

questions: The Teacher says to draw near to God to listen rather than to speak. What would change in your prayer or worship if listening came first?
Have you ever made a promise to God, or to someone else, carelessly? What does this chapter suggest about keeping or making such promises?
Verse 10 says the love of money never satisfies. Where have you seen more lead only to wanting more, and what does the Teacher offer as an alternative?
